learn.intro: From a tiny Munich party in 1919 to government in 1933: why did the Nazis fail in the 1920s, break through after 1929, and how did Hitler — who never won a majority in a free election — become Chancellor?

blocks.p: The German Workers' Party (DAP) was founded in Munich in January 1919 by Anton Drexler. Hitler, then an army political informant, joined in September 1919 and quickly became its star speaker. In February 1920 the party announced its 25-point programme — nationalist, anti-Semitic, anti-Versailles and vaguely anti-capitalist — and renamed itself the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP).

In July 1921 Hitler became party leader with near-total authority. The SA (Sturmabteilung) grew from the party's stewards in 1921; Ernst Röhm, an army officer with links to the Bavarian authorities and Freikorps, was vital in building it into a paramilitary force. The party bought its own newspaper, the Völkischer Beobachter, in 1920.

The Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch of 8–9 November 1923 tried to exploit the crisis year, copying Mussolini's march on Rome. Hitler counted on the Bavarian leaders Kahr, Lossow and Seisser, but they turned against him; the march through Munich was dispersed by police gunfire and 16 Nazis were killed. The failure taught Hitler that power would have to be won through the system.

sections.title: 2. Failure and survival, 1924–28

blocks.p: Hitler's trial (February–March 1924) gave him national publicity, and sympathetic judges gave him a five-year sentence of which he served about nine months in Landsberg prison. There he wrote Mein Kampf, setting out his ideas on race, Lebensraum and leadership, and decided on the 'legal path' to power.

The party was refounded in February 1925. At the Bamberg Conference (February 1926) Hitler defeated the northern, more socialist wing led by Gregor Strasser, establishing the Führerprinzip and his control of the programme. Joseph Goebbels switched to Hitler's side and became Gauleiter of Berlin.

A national organisation developed: regional Gaue, the Hitler Youth (1926), the SS as a personal bodyguard, and specialist groups for farmers, students and professions. But in the stable conditions of the mid-1920s the party struggled: in the Reichstag election of May 1928 it won only 2.6 per cent and 12 seats. It began to shift attention to rural, Protestant northern Germany, where agricultural depression was already hurting.

evidence: Sentence of 5 years; served about 9 months.

blocks.p: In 1929 the Nazis joined Alfred Hugenberg's DNVP and other nationalists in a campaign against the Young Plan. The referendum failed, but Hugenberg's newspapers gave Hitler national publicity and respectability with the conservative right.

The Wall Street Crash (October 1929) led American lenders to recall loans. German industrial output fell sharply and unemployment reached 6.1 million by January 1932. The Grand Coalition collapsed in March 1930 over unemployment-insurance contributions; Heinrich Brüning's government then governed increasingly through Article 48 decrees, and his deflationary cuts deepened the misery.

The Nazi vote rose to 18.3 per cent (107 seats) in September 1930 and 37.3 per cent (230 seats, the largest party) in July 1932. Goebbels's propaganda, mass rallies, Hitler's flights across Germany in 1932 and targeted messages to farmers, the middle classes and young voters were combined with SA intimidation and street violence. The Nazis drew support from across society, though most heavily from Protestant, rural and middle-class Germany.

The Communist vote also grew — reaching 16.9 per cent and 100 seats in November 1932 — which frightened the middle classes, industrialists and the elites, and made the Nazis look like the barrier against Bolshevism. In the Reichstag, Nazis and Communists together formed a negative majority that made parliamentary government almost impossible.

sections.title: 4. Coming to power, November 1932–March 1933

blocks.p: Hindenburg had replaced Brüning with Franz von Papen (June 1932), who lifted the ban on the SA and called the July election. Hitler refused anything less than the chancellorship. In November 1932 the Nazi vote fell to 33.1 per cent (196 seats), funds were low and the party seemed to have peaked.

General Kurt von Schleicher became Chancellor in December 1932 and tried to split the Nazis by offering Gregor Strasser the vice-chancellorship. Papen, seeking revenge, met Hitler in January 1933 and persuaded Hindenburg that a cabinet with Hitler as Chancellor, but only three Nazis, could be controlled by conservatives. Hitler was appointed on 30 January 1933.

Hitler then used state power to win support and crush opponents. On 3 February he reassured army leaders; on 20 February leading industrialists pledged money for the election campaign. Göring, as Prussian Interior Minister, enrolled SA and SS men as auxiliary police. After the Reichstag Fire (27 February), blamed on the Communist Marinus van der Lubbe, the Decree for the Protection of the People and the State (28 February) suspended civil liberties. In the election of 5 March the Nazis won 43.9 per cent (288 seats) — still not a majority without the DNVP.

The historians' debate: was Hitler's appointment the product of Nazi popularity and propaganda, of the economic crisis, of the structural weaknesses of Weimar, or — the most common emphasis — of the 'backstairs intrigue' of a small group of conservatives around Hindenburg who thought they could use him?

evidence: 30 January 1933: Hitler appointed; three Nazis in cabinet.
27–28 February 1933: Reichstag Fire and emergency decree.

misconceptions.right: He was appointed by Hindenburg. The Nazis never won a majority in a free election.

misconceptions.wrong: The Nazi vote kept rising until 1933.

misconceptions.right: Many unemployed voted KPD; Nazi support was strongest among the Protestant middle classes and rural voters.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of the impact of the Depression on Germany.

evidence.model: Papen persuaded Hindenburg in January 1933 that Hitler could be controlled in a cabinet with only three Nazis; Schleicher's attempt to split the party had failed.

evidence.model: Göring made SA and SS men auxiliary police; the Reichstag Fire Decree of 28 February suspended civil liberties; industrialists funded the campaign on 20 February.

flashcards.q: Name three ideas in the 25-point programme.
flashcards.a: Overturn Versailles; union of all Germans; anti-Semitic citizenship rules; land for expansion; some anti-capitalist demands.

flashcards.q: Why did the Munich Putsch fail?
flashcards.a: The Bavarian leaders Kahr, Lossow and Seisser turned against Hitler; poor planning; police fired on the march.

flashcards.q: How did Hitler benefit from his trial in 1924?
flashcards.a: National publicity; a lenient sentence served for about nine months; time to write Mein Kampf.

flashcards.q: Why did the Nazis do badly in 1924–28?
flashcards.a: Economic stability and the success of Stresemann's policies reduced the appeal of extremists.

flashcards.q: What were Brüning's economic policies and their effect?
flashcards.a: Deflation — spending and wage cuts — which deepened unemployment and earned him the name 'hunger chancellor'.

flashcards.q: Give three Nazi methods of winning support 1930–32.
flashcards.a: Goebbels's propaganda; mass rallies and Hitler's flights; targeted messages to groups; SA marches and intimidation.

flashcards.q: Which groups voted Nazi most heavily?
flashcards.a: Protestant, rural and middle-class Germans; but support came from across society.

flashcards.q: What was Schleicher's plan in December 1932?
flashcards.a: To split the Nazis by offering Gregor Strasser a post and win union support — it failed.

flashcards.q: Why did Hindenburg finally appoint Hitler?
flashcards.a: Persuaded by Papen and his advisers that a cabinet with only three Nazis could control him, and to end the political deadlock.
3 Feb: Hitler reassured army leaders. 20 Feb: industrialists pledged money for the Nazi election campaign.

flashcards.q: Why did the March 1933 election show the limits of Nazi support?
flashcards.a: Even with terror and propaganda the Nazis won 43.9% — not a majority without the DNVP.
Built the SA into a paramilitary force using his army and Freikorps contacts.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q:
Historians differ in their judgements about why Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933.
‘Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933 mainly because of the political intrigue of the conservative elites.’
Assess this view using your own knowledge of the issue.

model.t: In line with my judgement, the intrigue of the conservative elites was the decisive reason. In November 1932 the Nazi vote had fallen to 33.1 per cent and the party was short of money; it was Papen's meeting with Hitler in January 1933 and his persuasion of Hindenburg that turned a declining movement into a government.
model.n: Most important factor: point linked to the judgement + precise evidence (statistic, people, date).

model.t: A dissenting view might point to the 37.3 per cent won in July 1932, arguing that without mass support no conservative would have considered Hitler at all.

On the balance however, mass support gave Hitler a claim to power but not power itself: Hindenburg refused him the chancellorship in August 1932 despite that result. Judged by effectiveness, only the elites could make the appointment. Thus we must assert that intrigue was the most important reason.
model.n: Why it still wins + criterion + sustained judgement.
